title: 249 bots, 2,468 closed trades, profit factor 0.38. Down $392k. Here's the whole dashboard.
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
I've been running a paper fleet for about a month to stress-test a backtesting engine I'm building. 249 bots across 5 desks, everything on real quotes, no real money.

It's down $392,286 all-time. 42% win rate, profit factor 0.38 — so for every dollar it lost it made 38 cents back. Worst single day was −$173,070. Right now there's $5.29M of open risk sitting across 224 positions.

Recording is the whole thing, unedited. Desks, open trades, closed trades, the bots, the live terminal. I didn't cut out the red.

Two things I've actually learned from it, in case they're useful to anyone else:

A 42% win rate isn't the problem. Profit factor 0.38 is. The losers are roughly two and a half times the winners and no hit rate fixes that.

And open risk is the number I wasn't watching. $5.29M exposed against equity that's already down — I'd been looking at realised P&L, which tells you what already happened rather than what can still happen to you.

Genuinely curious what you'd look at first with a fleet this size. My instinct is that most of these bots are the same trade wearing different names, and the concentration is doing more damage than any single strategy.

comments.author: Equal-Collection-137
comments.body:
The issue I keep seeing is that pure technical analysis only works in a (fictional) purely speculative market that has no fundamental impactors. 

Institutions trade on mostly knowledge with a little bit of technical to understand the economics of it. 

How does your fleet handle fundamentals?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Honest answer: it mostly doesn't. The fleet is technical rules on price and volume. The one fundamentals-shaped thing in the engine is an earnings calendar (SEC 8-K filing dates), which a rule can use to skip the days around a print, and the grade reports what share of trades were held through earnings so you can see the exposure. No revenue, no valuations, no news. I agree that is a real hole, and it is one reason the fleet is down: a chart pattern does not know a guidance cut is coming. I would rather say that plainly than bolt on a sentiment feed and call it fundamentals.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Ha, fair. I do use it to write, and I am not going to pretend otherwise in a sub about AI trading. The bit that is mine is the answer: the earnings calendar is real, it is 8-K filing dates, the fleet really is technical rules only, and the hole really is a hole. I would rather be caught using a writing tool than caught inventing a fundamentals feature we do not have.

comments.author: LatterRain5
comments.body: How do u run 249 bots at the same time? U mean u have 249 scripts running simultaneously? Does the brokerage allow that many api connections? I'm running via ibkr and I think the maximum connection allow is 32 scripts, ie 32 client ID connected thru api. Can you share more about your setup?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: I used quantradin it is simulated environment for building trading bots

replies.author: LatterRain5
replies.body: Simulated? Does it trade live via paper/demo or just pure backtesting kind of simulation?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: To be precise, since "live" is doing a lot of work in my earlier answer: it is a paper desk on live quotes. Bots are walked against real-time bars, fills print at the real bid or ask, positions are marked around the clock and options settle at expiry, but no order ever reaches a broker and there is no real money. That is also why there is no API connection cap: one process walks all 249, nothing goes through IBKR.

replies.author: LatterRain5
replies.body: Then this is half baked bro. Until u send orders (via api to ibkr on paper trading, no real money) all these tests are as good as running backtest. U think u fill at mid-price, but reality is different. One of the biggest issue isn't just fill but the idiosyncratic nature of ibkr which often fail to fill the orders or double fill due to lag.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
You are right, and the sentence you are pushing on was mine, so let me fix it instead of defending it.

"Fills print at the real bid or ask" was too broad. It holds on the options path — a measured two-sided OPRA quote, buy the ask, sell the bid, never the mid. It does not describe most of my book. I counted this morning: 26,302 of 29,505 positions are equities, and an equity fill has no spread modeled at all. Signal on bar i, enter at the next bar's open, mark at the daily close. Not mid, but not bid/ask either, and my phrasing implied a precision the stock side does not have. The most flattering path of the three is credit structures, which mark off a Black-Scholes model price — a theoretical mid. 237 positions sitting on that right now. Labeled, but it is the one I trust least.

On the broker point I have no rebuttal. Nothing I run touches an order book. No queue position, no partials, no rejects, no double fill because the gateway lagged. That entire class of failure is invisible to me, and it is exactly the class that eats an edge. A paper desk on live quotes beats a backtest and loses to an order that actually got routed, and I have been sloppy about saying the second half out loud.

For whether the sim is flattering me: 24,908 closed trades, profit factor 0.37, down $1.06M. If it were tuned to be kind, it is doing a remarkable impression of the opposite.

comments.author: NefariousnessOpening
comments.body: Backtesting seems like a default for most of the people making agents or bots for trading. It seems to me like using old market data to make predictions doesn’t make sense. I think for a few use cases like maybe parameters on entries or something then backtesting would work. But for prediction it would be way more logical to reach for a concept derived from Markov or something. 249 bots is interesting, what is the reason for that number? What is the leverage gained from that many bots vs using fewer? What’s the goal of the backtesting engine? Or what problems does it solve?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Fair questions. Why 249: it was a stress test of the desk, not a portfolio. Every strategy family the engine supports, times a few parameter settings, times a few universes, so that if any one of them fired zero times or filled at a price no backtest ever offered, I would see it. That is the leverage from many bots: coverage, not returns. It found four real engine bugs in a month that no single bot would have surfaced.

  
On backtesting for prediction: agreed, it is a bad prediction tool. I use it as a rejection tool. It cannot tell you an idea will work; it can tell you an idea already failed on history it never saw, with fills at the ask and bid instead of the midpoint, and no look-ahead. Most of what people call a backtest fails on those two points, and that is the problem the engine is trying to solve: make the number you are looking at the same number you would have lived through. What you do for prediction on top of that, Markov or otherwise, is a separate layer.

replies.author: NefariousnessOpening
replies.body: There is a way I know of, just know a bit about it, yet to thoroughly examine it. But anyway a vector store enables a massive increase in the number of every aspect of the backtest. Might be a more efficient way to get the results of the 249 strategy families. Then I don’t know how this market works but I would say that if the news and other non capital market, numerical, sentiment analysis domain type stuff impacts the market than I immediately start to question the effectiveness of the ml ops that doesn’t include the data. I’m gonna ponder on what you said about an idea failing on a history it never saw. I think I don’t fully understand what that meant

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Let me try the "history it never saw" bit more plainly, because it is the whole argument and I said it badly.

  
Say you have ten years of data. The natural thing to do is try rules until one looks good on all ten years. The problem is you were the search: you tried a hundred variants and kept the one that fit. That rule now knows things about those ten years that it could not have known in advance, because you selected it after seeing the answer. Its backtest is not a prediction, it is a memory.

  
So instead you split. Build and tune on the first seven years only, and never look at the last three. Then run the finished rule on the last three once. If it holds up there, the edge survived contact with data that had no chance to influence how the rule was written. If it falls apart, you learned that in an afternoon instead of with money.

  
That is all my engine is doing, plus paying the real spread instead of the midpoint. Neither is clever. Both are things most published backtests skip, which is why the published numbers are always better than the live ones.

  
On the vector store point, I think you are describing something different from search speed: using embeddings so a strategy can be compared to prior market conditions rather than to a fixed rule. That is interesting and I have not built it. My honest hesitation is that it makes the same overfitting problem harder to see, not easier, because "this looks like March 2020" is exactly the kind of similarity that feels meaningful and is often just noise. But I would read a writeup if you build it.
